data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Ownership allocation systematically suppresses cross-cutting explanations because it creates an artificial sunk-cost bias: the owning lineage is incentivized to use its own primitives even when a rival's primitive is simpler, because using the rival's primitive would de-legitimize its parentage claim.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the owning lineage is not aware of the rival primitive, R=0 and no strategic suppression occurred.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the rival primitive is applicable but inferior, rejecting it is efficient, not suppressive.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If credit assignment does not track lineage ownership, there is no incentive to avoid rival primitives.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Lineage ownership is not just a search heuristic; it is a credit-assignment mechanism. The owning lineage gets credit for solving the problem. If it uses a rival's primitive, the credit is shared. This creates an incentive to avoid cross-cutting primitives even when they are available and superior. Suppression is not a structural barrier (vocabulary lacks the primitive) but a strategic one (lineage refuses to use the primitive). The evidence is a count of cases where the owning lineage *could have* adopted a rival primitive (the primitive was visible and applicable) but did not, and the resulting solution was weaker. Count R = number of rejected-but-applicable rival primitives. If R > 0, suppression is strategic, not just structural.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
